u:dsa-foundations-0-big-o-notation.title: Big-O notation
u:dsa-foundations-0-big-o-notation.summary: Big-O describes how an algorithm's cost grows with input size, ignoring constants.

blocks.text: **Big-O** captures the dominant growth term as the input size n grows, dropping constant factors and lower-order terms. It answers 'how does the work scale?', not 'how many milliseconds?'.
Big-O is an upper bound on growth. Compare algorithms by their order first; constants only matter when the orders tie.

mcqs.q: Which of these grows the fastest as n increases?
mcqs.explain: Exponential growth dominates every polynomial order.

mcqs.q: Big-O deliberately ignores:
mcqs.explain: It describes asymptotic growth, not exact operation counts.

mcqs.q: A single loop that scans an array of n items once is:
mcqs.explain: The work grows in direct proportion to n.

u:dsa-foundations-1-time-vs-space-comple.title: Time vs space complexity
u:dsa-foundations-1-time-vs-space-comple.summary: Every algorithm trades running time against extra memory; interviews ask about both.

blocks.text: **Time complexity** counts operations; **space complexity** counts the extra memory an algorithm allocates beyond its input. A hash map can turn an O(n^2) scan into O(n) time but costs O(n) space.
State both when you analyse a solution. 'O(n) time, O(1) extra space' is a stronger answer than time alone.
Recursion has a hidden space cost: the **call stack** uses O(depth) memory even if the code allocates nothing else.

mcqs.q: Space complexity measures:
options: Extra memory used beyond the input
mcqs.explain: It counts auxiliary memory the algorithm allocates.

mcqs.q: Using a hash set to detect duplicates in one pass trades:
mcqs.explain: O(n) space buys an O(n) instead of O(n^2) scan.

mcqs.q: A recursion 20 levels deep uses call-stack space of about:
mcqs.explain: Each pending call keeps a frame on the stack.

u:dsa-foundations-2-analysing-recursion.title: Analysing recursion
u:dsa-foundations-2-analysing-recursion.summary: Model a recursive routine as a recurrence, then solve it for the overall cost.

blocks.text: A recursive algorithm's cost is a **recurrence**: work at this level plus the cost of the subcalls. Merge sort splits in two and does O(n) to merge, giving T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n).

items: **Divide by a constant factor** each call (e.g. n/2) -> often O(log n) depth.
**Subtract one** each call (e.g. n-1) -> O(n) depth.
**Branching factor** multiplies work: two calls per level with no shrink -> O(2^n).

blocks.text: Total cost = (number of nodes in the recursion tree) x (work per node). Draw the tree when unsure.

mcqs.q: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) solves to:
mcqs.explain: Log n levels, each doing O(n) total work (merge sort).

mcqs.q: Naive Fibonacci recursion f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n-2) is:
mcqs.explain: The branching tree roughly doubles each level.

mcqs.q: Halving the input each recursive call typically gives a depth of:
mcqs.explain: You can halve n only about log2(n) times.

u:dsa-foundations-3-amortized-analysis.title: Amortized analysis
u:dsa-foundations-3-amortized-analysis.summary: Some operations are occasionally expensive but cheap on average across a sequence.

blocks.text: **Amortized cost** averages an operation's cost over a long run. A dynamic array's push is usually O(1), but occasionally O(n) when it doubles capacity and copies. Averaged over many pushes, each is O(1) amortized.
Amortized is not the same as average-case. It's a worst-case guarantee over a SEQUENCE of operations, with no probability assumptions.

mcqs.q: Appending to a dynamic array (with doubling) is:
mcqs.explain: Rare O(n) resizes average out to O(1) per push.

mcqs.q: Amortized analysis differs from average-case because it:
mcqs.explain: It's a guaranteed average over a sequence, not an expectation.

mcqs.q: A dynamic array resizes by:
mcqs.explain: Geometric growth keeps amortized push at O(1).

u:dsa-arrays-0-prefix-sums.title: Prefix sums
u:dsa-arrays-0-prefix-sums.summary: Precompute running totals so any range sum is answered in O(1).

blocks.text: A **prefix-sum** array stores pre[i] = sum of the first i elements. The sum of range [l, r] is then pre[r+1] - pre[l], answered in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.

pre[0] = 0
for i in range(n):
    pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i]
# sum of a[l..r] inclusive:
range_sum = pre[r+1] - pre[l]
The same idea extends to 2D (integral images) and to prefix XOR / prefix counts.

mcqs.q: After building a prefix-sum array, a range sum query costs:
mcqs.explain: Each query is a single subtraction.

mcqs.q: pre[i] is defined as the sum of:
mcqs.explain: That definition makes range sums a clean subtraction.

mcqs.q: Prefix sums are ideal when you have:
options: Many range-sum queries on a fixed array
mcqs.explain: Precomputation pays off across many queries.

u:dsa-arrays-1-two-pointers.title: Two pointers
u:dsa-arrays-1-two-pointers.summary: Walk two indices toward each other (or together) to avoid a nested loop.

blocks.text: The **two-pointer** pattern uses two indices that move based on a condition, turning many O(n^2) pair searches into O(n). Classic use: find a pair summing to a target in a **sorted** array by moving pointers inward.
The array being sorted is what makes the move decisions correct - each step provably discards no valid answer.

mcqs.q: Two pointers reduce a sorted-pair search from O(n^2) to:
mcqs.explain: Each pointer advances at most n times total.

mcqs.q: In the sorted two-sum, if the current sum is too small you:
mcqs.explain: A larger left value increases the sum.

mcqs.q: The opposite-ends two-pointer trick usually requires the array to be:
options: A power of two in length
mcqs.explain: Sorted order justifies which pointer to move.

u:dsa-arrays-2-sliding-window-fixed-size.title: Sliding window (fixed size)
u:dsa-arrays-2-sliding-window-fixed-size.summary: Slide a window of constant width, updating the answer in O(1) per step.

blocks.text: For a **fixed-size window** of width k, compute the first window, then slide: add the entering element and remove the leaving one. This gives O(n) instead of recomputing each window in O(k).

window = sum(a[:k])
best = window
for i in range(k, n):
    window += a[i] - a[i-k]   # add new, drop old
    best = max(best, window)

mcqs.q: Sliding a fixed window and updating incrementally makes the scan:
mcqs.explain: Each element enters and leaves the window once.

mcqs.q: When the window slides one step you:
options: Add the entering element and subtract the leaving one
mcqs.explain: Incremental update is the whole point of the pattern.

mcqs.q: Fixed-size sliding window applies when the subarray length is:
mcqs.explain: A fixed k is what makes the O(1) update possible.

u:dsa-arrays-3-sliding-window-variable-s.title: Sliding window (variable size)
u:dsa-arrays-3-sliding-window-variable-s.summary: Grow and shrink a window to satisfy a constraint, e.g. longest substring without repeats.

blocks.text: A **variable window** expands its right edge to include more, and shrinks its left edge whenever a constraint breaks. Track the best valid window seen. It answers 'longest/shortest subarray with property X' in O(n).

items: Expand `right`, updating counts/sums.
While the window is invalid, advance `left` to restore validity.
Record the best valid window at each step.

blocks.text: A hash map of counts inside the window tells you when to shrink (e.g. a character repeated).

mcqs.q: A variable-size window shrinks from the left when:
mcqs.explain: Shrinking restores validity before recording the answer.

mcqs.q: 'Longest substring without repeating characters' is solved with:
mcqs.explain: The window grows/shrinks to stay repeat-free.

mcqs.q: Both pointers only ever move forward, so the total work is:
mcqs.explain: Each index advances at most n times.

u:dsa-arrays-4-hashing-and-frequency-map.title: Hashing & frequency maps
u:dsa-arrays-4-hashing-and-frequency-map.summary: Hash maps give average O(1) lookup, powering counting and dedup patterns.

blocks.text: A **hash map / set** stores keys with average O(1) insert and lookup. It converts 'have I seen this?' and 'how many of each?' questions from O(n^2) to O(n).

items: **Seen-set**: detect duplicates or complements in one pass.
**Frequency map**: count occurrences for anagrams, majority element, top-K.
**Index map**: remember where a value last appeared.

blocks.text: Hash operations are O(1) on average but O(n) worst case under many collisions; usually fine for interviews.

mcqs.q: Average-case lookup in a hash map is:
mcqs.explain: Hashing jumps to the bucket directly on average.

mcqs.q: Counting character frequencies to compare anagrams runs in:
mcqs.explain: One pass fills the frequency map.

mcqs.q: A hash set is the natural tool for:
options: Detecting whether a value was already seen
mcqs.explain: Membership tests are its core O(1) strength.

u:dsa-arrays-5-kadane-s-algorithm.title: Kadane's algorithm
u:dsa-arrays-5-kadane-s-algorithm.summary: Find the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in a single O(n) pass.

blocks.text: **Kadane's algorithm** keeps a running best-ending-here sum: at each element, either extend the previous subarray or start fresh at the current element, whichever is larger. Track the global best.

best = cur = a[0]
for x in a[1:]:
    cur = max(x, cur + x)   # extend or restart
    best = max(best, cur)
The decision `max(x, cur + x)` is the heart of it: a negative running sum is never worth carrying forward.

mcqs.q: Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum-sum:
mcqs.explain: It requires the elements to be contiguous.

mcqs.q: At each step Kadane's chooses between:
options: Extending the current subarray or starting a new one
mcqs.explain: max(x, cur+x) encodes exactly that choice.

mcqs.q: Kadane's runs in:
mcqs.explain: A single pass with two running variables.

u:dsa-binary-search-0-binary-search-fund.title: Binary search fundamentals
u:dsa-binary-search-0-binary-search-fund.summary: Halve a sorted search space each step to find a target in O(log n).

blocks.text: **Binary search** works on a **sorted** (or monotonic) space. Compare the target to the middle; discard the half that cannot contain it. Each step halves the range, giving O(log n).

lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2   # avoids overflow
    if a[mid] == target: return mid
    if a[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
return -1
Compute mid as lo + (hi - lo)//2, not (lo+hi)//2, to avoid integer overflow in languages with fixed-width ints.

mcqs.q: Binary search requires the data to be:
mcqs.explain: Ordering is what lets you discard half safely.

mcqs.q: Each comparison in binary search:
mcqs.explain: That halving yields the O(log n) bound.

mcqs.q: `mid = lo + (hi - lo)//2` is preferred because it:
mcqs.explain: lo+hi can overflow fixed-width integers.

u:dsa-binary-search-1-lower-and-upper-bo.title: Lower & upper bound
u:dsa-binary-search-1-lower-and-upper-bo.summary: Find the first/last valid position, not just an exact match.

blocks.text: **Lower bound** returns the first index whose value is >= target; **upper bound** returns the first index whose value is > target. These handle duplicates and 'insert position' questions that plain binary search can't.
The count of a value equals upperBound(x) - lowerBound(x). Both are O(log n).
Frame boundary searches as 'find the first index where a predicate becomes true' - a robust, bug-resistant template.

mcqs.q: Lower bound returns the first element that is:
mcqs.explain: It's the first position not less than the target.

mcqs.q: The number of occurrences of x in a sorted array is:
mcqs.explain: The gap between the two bounds counts the duplicates.

mcqs.q: Boundary binary searches are best framed as finding:
options: The first index where a predicate turns true
mcqs.explain: Predicate framing avoids off-by-one bugs.

u:dsa-binary-search-2-binary-search-on-t.title: Binary search on the answer
u:dsa-binary-search-2-binary-search-on-t.summary: When the answer is monotonic, binary-search the value itself.

blocks.text: If a candidate answer has a **monotonic** feasibility (once it works, all larger/smaller values also work), binary-search over the answer range and test feasibility with a helper. Classic: minimum ship capacity, Koko eating bananas, split array largest sum.

items: Identify the answer's numeric range [lo, hi].
Write feasible(x): can we achieve the goal with value x?
Binary-search for the smallest (or largest) feasible x.

blocks.text: The trigger phrase is 'minimize the maximum' or 'maximize the minimum' with a checkable condition.

mcqs.q: Binary search on the answer needs the feasibility check to be:
mcqs.explain: Monotonicity lets you discard half the value range.

mcqs.q: 'Minimize the maximum load' style problems often use:
mcqs.explain: You search the answer space and test feasibility.

mcqs.q: The feasible(x) helper typically runs in:
options: O(n), giving O(n log range) overall
mcqs.explain: A linear check inside a log-range search.

u:dsa-binary-search-3-search-in-rotated-.title: Search in rotated sorted array
u:dsa-binary-search-3-search-in-rotated-.summary: A rotated sorted array is still searchable in O(log n) by finding the sorted half.

blocks.text: A sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot has one **sorted half** on either side of mid. At each step, determine which half is sorted, check whether the target lies within it, and recurse into the correct side - still O(log n).
Compare a[lo] with a[mid] to decide which half is sorted, then test if the target is inside that sorted range.

mcqs.q: In a rotated sorted array, at any mid there is always:
mcqs.explain: Rotation leaves one side fully ordered.

mcqs.q: Searching a rotated sorted array can still be done in:
mcqs.explain: You keep halving by identifying the sorted side.

mcqs.q: You decide which half is sorted by comparing:
mcqs.explain: That comparison reveals the ordered side.

u:dsa-sorting-0-sorting-algorithms-overv.title: Sorting algorithms overview
u:dsa-sorting-0-sorting-algorithms-overv.summary: Know the trade-offs: comparison sorts are O(n log n); some sorts are stable, some in-place.

blocks.text: Comparison-based sorts can't beat **O(n log n)** in the worst case. The practical ones differ in stability and memory:
A **stable** sort preserves the relative order of equal keys - essential when sorting by multiple criteria.

mcqs.q: The best worst-case time for a comparison sort is:
mcqs.explain: Comparison sorting has an n log n lower bound.

mcqs.q: A stable sort guarantees that equal elements:
mcqs.explain: Stability matters for multi-key sorting.

mcqs.q: Which common sort has O(n^2) worst case despite being fast in practice?
mcqs.explain: Bad pivots degrade quicksort to quadratic.

u:dsa-sorting-1-merge-sort-and-divide-an.title: Merge sort & divide and conquer
u:dsa-sorting-1-merge-sort-and-divide-an.summary: Split, sort each half, and merge - the archetypal divide-and-conquer sort.

blocks.text: **Merge sort** splits the array in half, recursively sorts each half, then **merges** the two sorted halves in O(n). Total: O(n log n) time, O(n) space, and it is stable.
The **merge** step is reusable on its own - e.g. counting inversions, or merging k sorted lists.
Divide and conquer = split into subproblems, solve recursively, combine. Merge sort's 'combine' is the merge.

mcqs.q: Merge sort's time complexity is:
options: O(n log n) in all cases
mcqs.explain: It always splits evenly and merges in linear time.

mcqs.q: Merge sort is:
mcqs.explain: It preserves equal-key order but needs O(n) extra space.

mcqs.q: The merge step of two sorted halves runs in:
mcqs.explain: A single linear pass with two pointers.

u:dsa-sorting-2-quick-sort-and-quicksele.title: Quick sort & quickselect
u:dsa-sorting-2-quick-sort-and-quicksele.summary: Partition around a pivot; average O(n log n) sort, and O(n) selection.

blocks.text: **Quick sort** picks a pivot, **partitions** elements into < pivot and > pivot, then recurses on each side. Average O(n log n); worst O(n^2) on bad pivots (mitigated by randomising the pivot).
**Quickselect** reuses partitioning to find the k-th smallest element in **average O(n)** by recursing into only the side that contains k.
Already-sorted input with a naive first-element pivot triggers quicksort's O(n^2) worst case - randomise or use median-of-three.

mcqs.q: Quick sort's average time complexity is:
mcqs.explain: Balanced partitions give log n depth of O(n) work.

mcqs.q: Quickselect finds the k-th smallest element in average:
mcqs.explain: It recurses into only one partition each step.

mcqs.q: Quicksort's O(n^2) worst case is usually avoided by:
mcqs.explain: Random pivots make bad splits vanishingly unlikely.

u:dsa-sorting-3-non-comparison-sorts.title: Non-comparison sorts
u:dsa-sorting-3-non-comparison-sorts.summary: Counting and radix sort beat O(n log n) when keys are small integers.

blocks.text: **Counting sort** tallies occurrences of each key and rebuilds the array in O(n + k) for keys in range [0, k]. **Radix sort** applies counting sort digit by digit for larger integers, O(d * (n + b)).
These bypass the n log n bound because they don't compare elements - they use the keys as array indices. They only work for bounded integer (or fixed-length) keys.

mcqs.q: Counting sort runs in:
options: O(n + k) for keys in [0, k]
mcqs.explain: It tallies counts and rebuilds linearly.

mcqs.q: Non-comparison sorts can beat O(n log n) because they:
options: Use keys as indices instead of comparing
mcqs.explain: Avoiding comparisons sidesteps the lower bound.

mcqs.q: Counting sort is only practical when the key range k is:
mcqs.explain: A giant k makes its O(n+k) memory/time blow up.

u:dsa-sorting-4-custom-comparators-and-s.title: Custom comparators & stability
u:dsa-sorting-4-custom-comparators-and-s.summary: Sort by multiple keys with a comparator; rely on stability for tie-breaks.

blocks.text: A **comparator** defines the order for complex objects: e.g. sort by score descending, then by name ascending. Return negative/zero/positive (or a tuple key) to encode the order.

# Python: sort by score desc, then name asc
items.sort(key=lambda x: (-x.score, x.name))
Composite tuple keys are the cleanest way to express multi-level sorts and avoid comparator bugs.

mcqs.q: A comparator that returns a negative value means the first item should come:
mcqs.explain: Negative means 'first sorts earlier'.

mcqs.q: To sort by score descending then name ascending, a clean key is:
mcqs.explain: Negating score flips only that field's order.

mcqs.q: Stability lets you achieve a multi-key sort by:
options: Sorting only once by the main key
Sorting by the least significant key first
mcqs.explain: Stable passes from least to most significant preserve earlier order.

u:dsa-linked-lists-0-linked-list-fundame.title: Linked list fundamentals
u:dsa-linked-lists-0-linked-list-fundame.summary: Nodes linked by pointers give O(1) insert/delete but O(n) access.

blocks.text: A **linked list** stores each element in a node holding a value and a pointer to the next node. Insertion/deletion at a known position is O(1) (just relink pointers), but random access is O(n) - you must walk from the head.
A **doubly** linked list also stores a prev pointer, enabling O(1) deletion given only the node.

mcqs.q: Accessing the i-th element of a singly linked list is:
mcqs.explain: You must traverse from the head.

mcqs.q: Inserting a node after a known node is:
mcqs.explain: It's just a couple of pointer reassignments.

mcqs.q: A doubly linked list adds a pointer to enable:
options: O(1) deletion given only the node
mcqs.explain: The prev pointer lets you relink without a scan.

u:dsa-linked-lists-1-reversing-a-linked-.title: Reversing a linked list
u:dsa-linked-lists-1-reversing-a-linked-.summary: Reverse pointers iteratively with three references, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: To **reverse** a singly linked list, walk the list re-pointing each node's next to its predecessor, using three pointers: prev, cur, and a saved next.

prev = None
cur = head
while cur:
    nxt = cur.next   # save
    cur.next = prev  # reverse the link
    prev = cur       # advance
    cur = nxt
return prev  # new head

mcqs.q: Iterative reversal of a linked list uses extra space of:
mcqs.explain: Only a few pointers, no extra data structure.

mcqs.q: Before overwriting cur.next you must:
mcqs.explain: Otherwise you lose the rest of the list.

mcqs.q: After the loop, the new head of the reversed list is:
mcqs.explain: cur has run off the end; prev is the last node visited.

u:dsa-linked-lists-2-fast-and-slow-point.title: Fast & slow pointers
u:dsa-linked-lists-2-fast-and-slow-point.summary: Two pointers at different speeds detect cycles and find the middle in one pass.

blocks.text: **Floyd's tortoise and hare**: advance one pointer by 1 and another by 2. If they meet, there's a **cycle**; if the fast one reaches the end, there isn't. The same pattern finds the **middle** node (slow lands at the middle when fast hits the end).
Cycle detection this way uses O(1) space - no visited set needed.
To find the cycle's start, after they meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance both by 1; they meet at the cycle entry.

mcqs.q: Floyd's cycle detection uses extra space of:
mcqs.explain: Just two pointers, no visited set.

mcqs.q: Moving one pointer at speed 2 and another at speed 1, in a cyclic list they will:
mcqs.explain: The faster pointer laps the slower inside the cycle.

mcqs.q: When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at:
mcqs.explain: Half speed means half the distance covered.

u:dsa-linked-lists-3-merging-and-dummy-n.title: Merging & dummy nodes
u:dsa-linked-lists-3-merging-and-dummy-n.summary: A dummy head node removes edge cases when building or merging lists.

blocks.text: Merging two sorted lists is like the merge step of merge sort: repeatedly attach the smaller head. A **dummy** (sentinel) node before the real head avoids special-casing the empty result and simplifies the code.

dummy = Node(0); tail = dummy
while a and b:
    if a.val <= b.val: tail.next, a = a, a.next
    else: tail.next, b = b, b.next
    tail = tail.next
tail.next = a or b
return dummy.next

mcqs.q: A dummy head node is used to:
mcqs.explain: It gives tail.next a valid target from the start.

mcqs.q: Merging two sorted linked lists runs in:
mcqs.explain: One linear pass over both lists.

mcqs.q: After merging, the real head is:
mcqs.explain: The dummy is discarded; its next is the merged head.

u:dsa-stacks-queues-0-stacks-lifo.title: Stacks (LIFO)
u:dsa-stacks-queues-0-stacks-lifo.summary: Last-in-first-out; the tool for matching, undo, and DFS.

blocks.text: A **stack** supports push and pop at one end - **last in, first out**. It underlies balanced-parenthesis checks, expression evaluation, undo history, and iterative DFS.
Whenever a problem involves 'most recent unmatched' or nesting, reach for a stack first.

mcqs.q: A stack follows which ordering?
mcqs.explain: Push and pop happen at the same end.

mcqs.q: Balanced-parentheses checking naturally uses a:
mcqs.explain: You pop the matching opener for each closer.

mcqs.q: Push and pop on a stack are:
mcqs.explain: Both operate at the top in constant time.

u:dsa-stacks-queues-1-queues-and-deques-.title: Queues & deques (FIFO)
u:dsa-stacks-queues-1-queues-and-deques-.summary: First-in-first-out; deques allow O(1) at both ends.

blocks.text: A **queue** is first-in-first-out - the tool for BFS and scheduling. A **deque** (double-ended queue) allows O(1) push/pop at both ends and powers sliding-window-maximum and monotonic-queue patterns.
Implement a queue with a linked list or a circular buffer; a plain array dequeue from the front is O(n).

mcqs.q: A queue follows which ordering?
mcqs.explain: You remove from the front, add at the back.

mcqs.q: BFS relies on a:
mcqs.explain: FIFO order visits nodes in increasing distance.

mcqs.q: A deque supports O(1) operations at:
mcqs.explain: That's what 'double-ended' means.

u:dsa-stacks-queues-2-monotonic-stack.title: Monotonic stack
u:dsa-stacks-queues-2-monotonic-stack.summary: Keep a stack in increasing/decreasing order to answer 'next greater' style queries in O(n).

blocks.text: A **monotonic stack** maintains elements in sorted (increasing or decreasing) order. As you scan, pop elements that violate the order - each pop resolves an answer. It solves next-greater-element, daily-temperatures, and largest-rectangle-in-histogram in O(n).
Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so despite the inner while-loop the total work is O(n).

mcqs.q: A monotonic stack solves next-greater-element in:
mcqs.explain: Amortized O(1) per element - each is pushed/popped once.

mcqs.q: Elements are popped from a monotonic stack when they:
mcqs.explain: Each violating pop finalises that element's answer.

mcqs.q: Largest rectangle in a histogram is efficiently solved with a:
mcqs.explain: The stack tracks bars in increasing height.

u:dsa-stacks-queues-3-next-greater-eleme.title: Next greater element
u:dsa-stacks-queues-3-next-greater-eleme.summary: For each item, find the nearest larger item to its right using a monotonic stack.

blocks.text: **Next greater element**: scan right to left, keeping a decreasing stack of candidates. Pop everything <= the current value; the stack top (if any) is the answer; then push the current value.

mcqs.q: Scanning right-to-left with a decreasing stack, the answer for i is:
options: The stack top after popping smaller-or-equal values
mcqs.explain: Remaining top is the nearest greater to the right.

mcqs.q: Values <= the current element are popped because they:
options: Can never be a future element's next-greater over the current
mcqs.explain: A larger, closer element dominates them.

mcqs.q: The overall complexity is:
mcqs.explain: Each index is pushed and popped once.

u:dsa-backtracking-0-backtracking-templa.title: Backtracking template
u:dsa-backtracking-0-backtracking-templa.summary: Explore choices, recurse, then undo - a systematic search of all valid configurations.

blocks.text: **Backtracking** builds a solution incrementally and abandons a path ('backtracks') as soon as it can't lead to a valid answer. The template: choose -> explore (recurse) -> un-choose.
Pruning invalid branches early is what makes backtracking tractable versus brute-forcing every combination.

mcqs.q: The three-step backtracking pattern is:
mcqs.explain: You undo the choice after exploring it.

mcqs.q: Backtracking becomes efficient mainly through:
mcqs.explain: Early pruning cuts the search tree dramatically.

mcqs.q: Backtracking is a form of:
options: Depth-first search over the solution space
mcqs.explain: It dives down one path fully before trying others.

u:dsa-backtracking-1-subsets-and-combina.title: Subsets & combinations
u:dsa-backtracking-1-subsets-and-combina.summary: Generate all subsets (2^n) or fixed-size combinations by include/exclude decisions.

blocks.text: Every element is either **in or out** of a subset, giving 2^n subsets. Backtracking with an 'include this index or skip it' decision (or a start-index loop) enumerates them without duplicates.
For combinations, pass a start index so you only ever move forward - this prevents generating the same set in a different order.

mcqs.q: The number of subsets of an n-element set is:
mcqs.explain: Each element is independently in or out.

mcqs.q: To avoid duplicate combinations, the recursion should:
options: Only consider indices from a moving start point
mcqs.explain: A forward-only start index fixes an ordering.

mcqs.q: Generating all subsets is inherently:
mcqs.explain: There are 2^n subsets to produce.

u:dsa-backtracking-2-permutations.title: Permutations
u:dsa-backtracking-2-permutations.summary: Arrange all n elements in every order (n!) by swapping or a used-set.

blocks.text: **Permutations** are all orderings of the elements - n! of them. Backtracking picks an unused element for each position (tracked by a used[] array or by swapping in place), then recurses.
With duplicate values, sort first and skip a value equal to its predecessor at the same level to avoid repeated permutations.

mcqs.q: The number of permutations of n distinct elements is:
mcqs.explain: n choices, then n-1, and so on.

mcqs.q: To generate permutations, each position picks:
mcqs.explain: A used-set (or swap) prevents reuse.

mcqs.q: To de-duplicate permutations of a multiset you should:
options: Sort and skip equal siblings at the same level
mcqs.explain: Skipping equal choices per level removes repeats.

u:dsa-backtracking-3-constraint-backtrac.title: Constraint backtracking (N-Queens)
u:dsa-backtracking-3-constraint-backtrac.summary: Place items under constraints, pruning conflicts as you go.

blocks.text: Problems like **N-Queens** and **Sudoku** place items subject to constraints. Backtracking tries a placement, checks it against constraints (column, diagonals for queens), recurses if valid, and undoes on dead ends.
Track occupied columns and diagonals in sets for O(1) conflict checks instead of rescanning the board.

mcqs.q: N-Queens uses backtracking to:
options: Place a queen per row, pruning column/diagonal conflicts
mcqs.explain: Each row gets one queen; conflicts prune branches.

mcqs.q: Fast conflict checks for queens are done by:
options: Tracking used columns and diagonals in sets
Rescanning the whole board each time
mcqs.explain: Sets give O(1) membership tests.

mcqs.q: When no valid placement exists in a row, the algorithm:
mcqs.explain: It undoes the last choice and tries another.

u:dsa-trees-0-binary-tree-traversals-dfs.title: Binary tree traversals (DFS)
u:dsa-trees-0-binary-tree-traversals-dfs.summary: Preorder, inorder, and postorder visit nodes in different useful orders.

blocks.text: Depth-first traversals of a binary tree differ by WHEN the node is processed relative to its children:

items: **Preorder** (node, left, right): copy/serialize a tree.
**Inorder** (left, node, right): yields sorted order for a BST.
**Postorder** (left, right, node): delete/free a tree, or compute from children up.

blocks.text: Inorder traversal of a binary SEARCH tree visits keys in ascending order - a very common test.

mcqs.q: Inorder traversal of a BST produces values in:
mcqs.explain: Left subtree < node < right subtree, recursively.

mcqs.q: Which traversal processes the node before its children?
mcqs.explain: Preorder is node, then left, then right.

mcqs.q: To compute a value that depends on both children first, use:
mcqs.explain: Postorder finishes children before the node.

u:dsa-trees-1-level-order-traversal-bfs.title: Level-order traversal (BFS)
u:dsa-trees-1-level-order-traversal-bfs.summary: Visit a tree level by level using a queue.

blocks.text: **Level-order** (breadth-first) traversal uses a **queue**: dequeue a node, process it, enqueue its children. Processing the queue one 'level size' at a time groups nodes by depth.
Snapshot the current queue length at the start of each level to separate levels cleanly.

mcqs.q: Level-order traversal is implemented with a:
mcqs.explain: FIFO order visits shallower nodes first.

mcqs.q: To group nodes by level, you process:
options: One queue-length batch at a time
mcqs.explain: The batch size equals that level's node count.

mcqs.q: BFS on a tree visits nodes in order of:
mcqs.explain: Each level is fully visited before the next.

u:dsa-trees-2-binary-search-trees.title: Binary search trees
u:dsa-trees-2-binary-search-trees.summary: An ordered tree giving O(log n) search/insert when balanced.

blocks.text: In a **binary search tree (BST)**, every node's left subtree holds smaller keys and its right subtree holds larger keys. Search, insert, and delete are O(h) where h is the height - O(log n) when balanced, but O(n) if it degenerates into a chain.
Inserting sorted data into a plain BST creates a linked-list-shaped tree with O(n) operations. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) prevent this.

mcqs.q: BST operations cost O(log n) only when the tree is:
mcqs.explain: Height drives cost; balance keeps height ~log n.

mcqs.q: In a BST, a node's left subtree contains keys that are:
mcqs.explain: That ordering enables binary-search-like descent.

mcqs.q: Inserting already-sorted keys into a naive BST yields:
mcqs.explain: Each key becomes the rightmost node.

u:dsa-trees-3-lowest-common-ancestor.title: Lowest common ancestor
u:dsa-trees-3-lowest-common-ancestor.summary: The deepest node that has two given nodes as descendants.

blocks.text: The **lowest common ancestor (LCA)** of two nodes is the deepest node that is an ancestor of both. In a BST, walk down: if both targets are smaller go left, if both larger go right, otherwise the current node is the LCA. In a general binary tree, recurse and return the node where the two targets split.
General-tree LCA: a node is the LCA if one target is found in its left subtree and the other in its right.

mcqs.q: In a BST, you've found the LCA when the two targets:
options: Lie on opposite sides of the current node
mcqs.explain: The split point is the lowest common ancestor.

mcqs.q: In a general binary tree, the LCA is the node where:
options: The two targets are found in different subtrees
mcqs.explain: That is the deepest node containing both.

mcqs.q: LCA in a balanced BST runs in:
mcqs.explain: A single root-to-split descent.

u:dsa-trees-4-height-depth-and-diameter.title: Height, depth & diameter
u:dsa-trees-4-height-depth-and-diameter.summary: Height and diameter are computed bottom-up with a single postorder pass.

blocks.text: A node's **height** is the longest downward path to a leaf; **depth** is the distance from the root. The tree's **diameter** is the longest path between any two nodes. Compute height with postorder recursion, and track diameter = max(leftHeight + rightHeight) along the way - all in O(n).
Diameter need not pass through the root; checking left+right height at every node handles that.

mcqs.q: A tree's diameter is:
options: The longest path between any two nodes
mcqs.explain: It may not pass through the root.

mcqs.q: Height and diameter are computed in one:
mcqs.explain: Children's heights combine into the node's answer.

mcqs.q: At each node, a diameter candidate is:
mcqs.explain: That is the longest path bending at this node.

u:dsa-heaps-0-heap-fundamentals.title: Heap fundamentals
u:dsa-heaps-0-heap-fundamentals.summary: A binary heap gives O(log n) insert and O(1) peek of the min or max.

blocks.text: A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree (stored in an array) where each parent is <= (min-heap) or >= (max-heap) its children. The extreme element sits at the root: **peek is O(1)**, while insert and extract are **O(log n)** via sift-up/sift-down.
Building a heap from n elements is O(n) (heapify), better than n inserts at O(n log n).
A **priority queue** is the abstract 'always give me the most important item next' interface; a heap is its usual implementation.

mcqs.q: Peeking the minimum of a min-heap is:
mcqs.explain: The min is always at the root.

mcqs.q: Insert and extract on a heap are:
mcqs.explain: Sifting travels at most the tree height.

mcqs.q: Building a heap from n items via heapify is:
mcqs.explain: Bottom-up heapify beats n separate inserts.

u:dsa-heaps-1-top-k-pattern.title: Top-K pattern
u:dsa-heaps-1-top-k-pattern.summary: Maintain a heap of size K to find the K largest/smallest efficiently.

blocks.text: To find the **K largest** elements, keep a **min-heap of size K**: push each element, and pop the smallest when the heap exceeds K. What remains are the K largest, in O(n log K) time - far better than sorting when K is small.
Use a MIN-heap for the K LARGEST (so the smallest of your winners is the one to evict), and a max-heap for the K smallest.

mcqs.q: Finding the K largest elements with a size-K heap costs:
mcqs.explain: Each of n elements does O(log K) heap work.

mcqs.q: For the K largest elements you keep a:
mcqs.explain: The min at the root is the weakest survivor to evict.

mcqs.q: The Top-K heap approach beats full sorting when:
options: K is much smaller than n
mcqs.explain: Small K keeps the log K factor tiny.

u:dsa-heaps-2-two-heaps-running-median.title: Two heaps (running median)
u:dsa-heaps-2-two-heaps-running-median.summary: A max-heap and a min-heap split the data to yield the median in O(1).

blocks.text: To track the **median of a stream**, keep a **max-heap** of the lower half and a **min-heap** of the upper half, balanced in size. The median is the top of the larger heap (or the average of both tops). Insert is O(log n); median query is O(1).

items: Push to the correct half based on value.
Rebalance so the sizes differ by at most one.
Read the median from the heap top(s).

mcqs.q: The two-heaps median trick uses:
options: A max-heap for the low half and a min-heap for the high half
mcqs.explain: The two tops straddle the median.

mcqs.q: Querying the current median is:
mcqs.explain: It's just the heap top(s).

mcqs.q: After each insertion you must:
mcqs.explain: Sizes must stay within one of each other.

u:dsa-graphs-0-graph-representations.title: Graph representations
u:dsa-graphs-0-graph-representations.summary: Adjacency list vs matrix: pick based on density and the operations you need.

blocks.text: An **adjacency list** stores, per vertex, a list of its neighbours - O(V + E) space, ideal for sparse graphs. An **adjacency matrix** is a V x V grid - O(V^2) space, giving O(1) edge lookups, good for dense graphs.
Most interview graphs are sparse - default to an adjacency list.

mcqs.q: An adjacency list uses space:
mcqs.explain: It stores each edge once (or twice, undirected).

mcqs.q: An adjacency matrix answers 'is there an edge?' in:
mcqs.explain: Direct grid indexing.

mcqs.q: For a sparse graph you should prefer an:
mcqs.explain: It avoids the O(V^2) matrix cost.

u:dsa-graphs-1-breadth-first-search-bfs.title: Breadth-first search (BFS)
u:dsa-graphs-1-breadth-first-search-bfs.summary: Explore level by level with a queue; finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

blocks.text: **BFS** explores a graph in expanding rings from the source using a queue and a visited set. In an **unweighted** graph it finds the **shortest path** (fewest edges) to every reachable node in O(V + E).
Mark a node visited when you ENQUEUE it, not when you dequeue it, to avoid adding it multiple times.

mcqs.q: BFS in an unweighted graph finds:
mcqs.explain: Level-by-level expansion reaches nodes at increasing distance.

mcqs.q: BFS runs in:
mcqs.explain: Each vertex and edge is processed once.

mcqs.q: To prevent revisiting, mark a node visited when you:
mcqs.explain: Marking at enqueue avoids duplicate queue entries.

u:dsa-graphs-2-depth-first-search-dfs.title: Depth-first search (DFS)
u:dsa-graphs-2-depth-first-search-dfs.summary: Dive deep before backtracking; finds components, cycles, and paths.

blocks.text: **DFS** follows a path as far as possible before backtracking, via recursion or an explicit stack. It's the basis for counting **connected components**, detecting **cycles**, **topological sort**, and flood-fill. O(V + E).
Deep recursion can overflow the call stack on large graphs; an explicit stack avoids that.

mcqs.q: DFS explores by:
options: Going as deep as possible before backtracking
mcqs.explain: It fully explores one branch before the next.

mcqs.q: Counting connected components is naturally done with:
options: DFS or BFS from each unvisited node
mcqs.explain: Each traversal covers one whole component.

mcqs.q: DFS on a graph runs in:
mcqs.explain: Every vertex and edge is touched once.

u:dsa-graphs-3-topological-sort.title: Topological sort
u:dsa-graphs-3-topological-sort.summary: Order a DAG so every edge points forward; the schedule for dependencies.

blocks.text: A **topological sort** linearly orders the vertices of a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** so that every edge u->v has u before v. It answers 'in what order can I do tasks with prerequisites?'. Two methods: **Kahn's** (repeatedly remove in-degree-0 nodes) or DFS postorder reversed.
A topological order exists if and only if the graph has no cycle. Kahn's algorithm detects a cycle when it can't output all nodes.

mcqs.q: Topological sort applies only to:
mcqs.explain: A cycle makes a valid ordering impossible.

mcqs.q: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with:
mcqs.explain: Zero remaining prerequisites can go next.

mcqs.q: If a topological sort can't include all nodes, the graph has:
mcqs.explain: Leftover nodes form a dependency cycle.

u:dsa-graphs-4-shortest-paths-dijkstra-a.title: Shortest paths (Dijkstra & friends)
u:dsa-graphs-4-shortest-paths-dijkstra-a.summary: Dijkstra for non-negative weights; BFS for unweighted; Bellman-Ford for negatives.

blocks.text: For **weighted** shortest paths with **non-negative** edges, **Dijkstra's algorithm** greedily expands the closest unsettled node using a min-heap: O((V + E) log V). For unweighted graphs, plain BFS suffices. For graphs with **negative** edges, use **Bellman-Ford** (O(VE)), which also detects negative cycles.
Dijkstra is WRONG with negative edge weights - a later cheaper path can undercut a node already settled.

mcqs.q: Dijkstra's algorithm requires edge weights to be:
mcqs.explain: Negatives break its greedy settling guarantee.

mcqs.q: For shortest paths in an UNWEIGHTED graph, use:
mcqs.explain: Every edge has equal cost, so BFS is optimal and simpler.

mcqs.q: To handle negative edge weights (and detect negative cycles), use:
mcqs.explain: Bellman-Ford relaxes edges V-1 times and checks for further improvement.

u:dsa-graphs-5-union-find-dsu.title: Union-Find (DSU)
u:dsa-graphs-5-union-find-dsu.summary: Track connected sets with near-constant union and find operations.

blocks.text: **Union-Find / Disjoint Set Union (DSU)** maintains a partition of elements into sets, supporting **find** (which set?) and **union** (merge two sets). With **path compression** and **union by rank/size**, both run in near-constant amortized time (inverse Ackermann).
It powers **Kruskal's MST**, cycle detection in undirected graphs, and connectivity queries.
Path compression flattens the tree during find; union by rank keeps trees shallow. Use both together.

mcqs.q: Union-Find with path compression and union by rank is:
mcqs.explain: The amortized cost is inverse-Ackermann, effectively O(1).

mcqs.q: Union-Find is the natural tool for:
mcqs.explain: It answers 'are these in the same set?' fast.

mcqs.q: Path compression works by:
options: Pointing nodes directly at the root during find
mcqs.explain: Flattening keeps future finds fast.

u:dsa-graphs-6-minimum-spanning-tree.title: Minimum spanning tree
u:dsa-graphs-6-minimum-spanning-tree.summary: Connect all vertices with minimum total edge weight (Kruskal or Prim).

blocks.text: A **minimum spanning tree (MST)** connects all vertices of a weighted, connected, undirected graph with the least total edge weight and no cycles. **Kruskal's** sorts edges and adds the cheapest that doesn't form a cycle (using DSU); **Prim's** grows the tree from a seed using a min-heap.
Both are greedy and both give an optimal MST; Kruskal shines on sparse graphs, Prim on dense ones.

mcqs.q: An MST of a graph with V vertices has exactly:
mcqs.explain: A spanning tree connecting V nodes needs V-1 edges.

mcqs.q: Kruskal's algorithm uses which structure to avoid cycles?
mcqs.explain: DSU checks whether an edge joins two already-connected sets.

mcqs.q: Both Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms are:
mcqs.explain: Each repeatedly takes a locally cheapest safe edge.

u:dsa-dp-0-dp-fundamentals.title: DP fundamentals
u:dsa-dp-0-dp-fundamentals.summary: Solve overlapping subproblems once and reuse the results - memoization or tabulation.

blocks.text: **Dynamic programming** applies when a problem has **optimal substructure** (the optimum is built from optima of subproblems) and **overlapping subproblems** (the same subproblem recurs). You compute each subproblem once and cache it.

items: **Memoization** (top-down): recursion + a cache. Natural, computes only needed states.
**Tabulation** (bottom-up): fill a table in dependency order. No recursion overhead.

blocks.text: The recurrence (state + transition) is the whole battle. Define what a state means and how states combine.

mcqs.q: DP requires the problem to have:
mcqs.explain: Those two properties are what make caching pay off.

mcqs.q: Top-down DP is also called:
mcqs.explain: It's recursion plus a results cache.

mcqs.q: The hardest and most important part of a DP is:
mcqs.explain: Everything else follows from a correct recurrence.

u:dsa-dp-1-1d-dp-patterns.title: 1D DP patterns
u:dsa-dp-1-1d-dp-patterns.summary: Problems where each state depends on a few previous states (stairs, house robber).

blocks.text: Many DP problems reduce to a **1D array** where dp[i] depends on a constant number of earlier entries. Climbing stairs: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]. House robber: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + value[i]).
When dp[i] uses only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], you can drop the array and keep two rolling variables - O(1) space.

mcqs.q: Climbing stairs (1 or 2 steps) has the recurrence:
mcqs.explain: Ways to reach i = ways to i-1 plus ways to i-2.

mcqs.q: House robber's choice at house i is:
options: Skip it (dp[i-1]) or take it plus dp[i-2]
mcqs.explain: You can't rob adjacent houses.

mcqs.q: When dp[i] depends only on dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], space can be:
mcqs.explain: Only the last two values are needed.

u:dsa-dp-2-0-1-knapsack.title: 0/1 Knapsack
u:dsa-dp-2-0-1-knapsack.summary: Choose items with weights and values to maximise value under a capacity limit.

blocks.text: **0/1 Knapsack**: given items with weight and value and a capacity W, maximise total value taking each item at most once. State dp[i][w] = best value using the first i items within capacity w; each item is either skipped or taken.
The inner loop can run over a 1D array from high to low capacity to use O(W) space.

mcqs.q: In 0/1 knapsack, each item can be taken:
mcqs.explain: That's what '0/1' means - in or out.

mcqs.q: The 0/1 knapsack DP state dp[i][w] represents:
options: Best value using first i items within capacity w
mcqs.explain: It captures both item prefix and remaining capacity.

mcqs.q: For each item the transition chooses between:
mcqs.explain: Take vs skip is the 0/1 decision.

u:dsa-dp-3-unbounded-knapsack-and-coin-c.title: Unbounded knapsack & coin change
u:dsa-dp-3-unbounded-knapsack-and-coin-c.summary: Items reusable any number of times, e.g. minimum coins for an amount.

blocks.text: **Unbounded knapsack** allows each item unlimited times. **Coin change** is the classic: minimum coins to make an amount. dp[a] = 1 + min over coins c of dp[a - c]. Iterate amount outward; each coin can be reused.
The difference from 0/1: the transition looks at dp of the SAME item row (or the current dp array) because reuse is allowed.

mcqs.q: Coin change (min coins) has the recurrence:
options: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over coins c
mcqs.explain: You add one coin c to an optimal smaller amount.

mcqs.q: Unbounded knapsack differs from 0/1 in that items:
mcqs.explain: Reuse changes which dp state the transition reads.

mcqs.q: If no combination of coins makes the amount, the answer is:
mcqs.explain: Unreachable states stay at the 'impossible' sentinel.

u:dsa-dp-4-longest-common-subsequence.title: Longest common subsequence
u:dsa-dp-4-longest-common-subsequence.summary: The longest sequence appearing in order (not necessarily contiguous) in both strings.

blocks.text: **LCS** finds the longest subsequence common to two strings. dp[i][j] = LCS of prefixes a[:i], b[:j]. If the last characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). O(n*m).
A subsequence keeps order but allows gaps; a substring must be contiguous. LCS is about subsequences.

mcqs.q: A subsequence differs from a substring in that it:
mcqs.explain: Subsequences may skip characters but keep order.

mcqs.q: When the current characters match, LCS does:
mcqs.explain: A matched pair extends the diagonal subproblem.

mcqs.q: LCS of two length-n and length-m strings costs:
mcqs.explain: The DP table has n*m cells, each O(1).

u:dsa-dp-5-longest-increasing-subsequenc.title: Longest increasing subsequence
u:dsa-dp-5-longest-increasing-subsequenc.summary: The longest strictly increasing subsequence, in O(n^2) or O(n log n).

blocks.text: **LIS**: the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. The O(n^2) DP sets dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with a[j] < a[i]. A smarter O(n log n) method keeps a 'tails' array and binary-searches the position to replace.
The tails[] array isn't the actual subsequence - it stores the smallest possible tail for each achievable length.

mcqs.q: The optimal LIS algorithm runs in:
mcqs.explain: Patience/tails with binary search achieves n log n.

mcqs.q: The O(n log n) LIS uses binary search to:
options: Find where to place/replace in the tails array
mcqs.explain: Each element replaces the first tail >= it.

mcqs.q: The O(n^2) LIS recurrence extends the best dp[j] where:
mcqs.explain: You extend increasing subsequences ending earlier.

u:dsa-dp-6-grid-dp.title: Grid DP
u:dsa-dp-6-grid-dp.summary: Count paths or find optimal cost across a grid, moving in limited directions.

blocks.text: **Grid DP** solves 'unique paths', 'minimum path sum', and similar: dp[r][c] combines the cells you can arrive from (usually top and left). dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]) for minimum path sum.
Handle the first row and column as base cases (only one way in), then fill row by row. O(rows*cols).

mcqs.q: Minimum path sum's transition is:
mcqs.explain: You come from the cheaper of top/left.

mcqs.q: Grid DP over an R x C grid costs:
mcqs.explain: Each cell is computed once in O(1).

mcqs.q: The first row and column of a paths grid are:
options: Base cases with one way to reach each
mcqs.explain: There's a single route along an edge.

u:dsa-greedy-0-greedy-fundamentals.title: Greedy fundamentals
u:dsa-greedy-0-greedy-fundamentals.summary: Make the locally optimal choice at each step; correct only when it provably leads to a global optimum.

blocks.text: A **greedy algorithm** builds a solution by taking the best-looking choice at each step and never reconsidering. It's fast and simple but only correct when the problem has the **greedy-choice property** and **optimal substructure** - otherwise DP or search is needed.
Greedy is often WRONG. Coin change with arbitrary denominations can't be solved greedily (that's why it's a DP). Always justify why the greedy choice is safe.

mcqs.q: A greedy algorithm is guaranteed correct only when:
mcqs.explain: A locally optimal choice must lead to a global optimum.

mcqs.q: Coin change with arbitrary denominations is:
mcqs.explain: Greedy can overshoot; DP guarantees the minimum.

mcqs.q: Compared with DP, greedy algorithms are usually:
options: Faster but applicable to fewer problems
mcqs.explain: They skip reconsidering choices, so they're limited.

u:dsa-greedy-1-interval-scheduling-and-m.title: Interval scheduling & merging
u:dsa-greedy-1-interval-scheduling-and-m.summary: Sort intervals, then sweep to select the most or merge overlaps.

blocks.text: For **activity selection** (maximise non-overlapping intervals), sort by **end time** and greedily take each interval that starts after the last chosen one ends. For **merging intervals**, sort by **start time** and merge any that overlap the running interval.

items: Sort by end (selection) or start (merging).
Sweep left to right, keeping the last chosen/merged interval.
Take or merge based on overlap.

blocks.text: Sorting by the RIGHT key is what makes the greedy choice provably optimal - end time for selection, start time for merging.

mcqs.q: To select the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals, sort by:
mcqs.explain: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for others.

mcqs.q: To merge overlapping intervals, sort by:
mcqs.explain: Sorted starts let you merge in one sweep.

mcqs.q: Interval greedy algorithms typically cost:
options: O(n log n) (dominated by the sort)
mcqs.explain: The sweep is linear after sorting.

u:dsa-bits-0-bitwise-basics.title: Bitwise basics
u:dsa-bits-0-bitwise-basics.summary: AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts operate on individual bits in O(1).

blocks.text: Bitwise operators act on the binary representation: **AND** (&) keeps common 1s, **OR** (|) sets any 1, **XOR** (^) flips where bits differ, **NOT** (~) inverts, and **shifts** (<<, >>) multiply/divide by powers of two.
Bit operations are constant time and often replace arithmetic for speed or to encode small sets.

mcqs.q: x << 3 is equivalent to multiplying x by:
mcqs.explain: Shifting left by k multiplies by 2^k.

mcqs.q: To test whether bit i of x is set, use:
mcqs.explain: Shift the bit down and mask it.

mcqs.q: XOR of two bits is 1 exactly when the bits:
mcqs.explain: XOR means 'exclusive or' - different inputs.

u:dsa-bits-1-common-bit-tricks.title: Common bit tricks
u:dsa-bits-1-common-bit-tricks.summary: Clear the lowest set bit, count bits, and detect powers of two in O(1).

blocks.text: Handy identities:

items: **x & (x-1)** clears the lowest set bit (used to count set bits fast).
**x & -x** isolates the lowest set bit.
**x & (x-1) == 0** tests whether x is a power of two (for x > 0).

blocks.text: Repeatedly applying x &= (x-1) and counting iterations gives the popcount in O(number of set bits).

mcqs.q: x & (x - 1) has the effect of:
mcqs.explain: It's the core of the fast bit-count loop.

mcqs.q: For x > 0, x & (x - 1) == 0 tests whether x is:
mcqs.explain: Powers of two have exactly one set bit.

mcqs.q: x & -x isolates:
mcqs.explain: Two's complement makes -x flip bits above the lowest one.

u:dsa-bits-2-xor-patterns.title: XOR patterns
u:dsa-bits-2-xor-patterns.summary: XOR's self-cancelling property finds unique elements without extra space.

blocks.text: **XOR** has powerful properties: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and it's commutative/associative. XORing every element of an array where all but one appear twice leaves the **single unique** element - O(n) time, O(1) space.
XOR is the go-to trick for 'find the number that appears once' and for swapping without a temp variable.

mcqs.q: XOR of a value with itself gives:
mcqs.explain: x ^ x cancels to zero.

mcqs.q: XORing all elements where every number but one appears twice yields:
mcqs.explain: Pairs cancel, leaving the lone value.

mcqs.q: The single-number XOR trick uses extra space of:
mcqs.explain: Just one accumulator variable.

u:dsa-strings-0-string-fundamentals.title: String fundamentals
u:dsa-strings-0-string-fundamentals.summary: Strings are immutable in many languages; build them efficiently.

blocks.text: In languages like Java and Python, strings are **immutable** - each concatenation creates a new string. Building a long result by repeated concatenation is O(n^2); use a **builder/list** and join once for O(n).
A loop doing result += char on an immutable string is a classic hidden O(n^2). Collect parts and join at the end.

mcqs.q: Repeated concatenation onto an immutable string in a loop is:
mcqs.explain: Each += copies the whole growing string.

mcqs.q: The efficient way to build a big string is to:
mcqs.explain: One join pass is O(n).

mcqs.q: Strings being immutable means:
options: Modifying one creates a new string
mcqs.explain: In-place edits aren't allowed on immutables.

u:dsa-strings-1-palindromes-and-two-poin.title: Palindromes & two pointers
u:dsa-strings-1-palindromes-and-two-poin.summary: Check or expand palindromes with pointers from the ends or the centre.

blocks.text: A **palindrome** reads the same forwards and backwards. Verify with two pointers from both ends moving inward (O(n)). To find the **longest palindromic substring**, expand around each centre (2n-1 centres), O(n^2).
Expand-around-centre must handle both odd-length (single centre) and even-length (two-character centre) palindromes.

mcqs.q: Checking whether a string is a palindrome with two pointers is:
mcqs.explain: Pointers meet in the middle after n/2 comparisons.

mcqs.q: Expand-around-centre for longest palindromic substring is:
mcqs.explain: n centres, each expanding up to O(n).

mcqs.q: Expand-around-centre must consider centres that are:
options: Both single characters and character pairs
mcqs.explain: Even-length palindromes have a two-char centre.

u:dsa-strings-2-pattern-matching-kmp.title: Pattern matching (KMP)
u:dsa-strings-2-pattern-matching-kmp.summary: Find a pattern in text in O(n + m) by never re-examining matched characters.

blocks.text: The **Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP)** algorithm searches for a pattern in text in **O(n + m)**. It precomputes a **prefix function (failure table)** telling how far to fall back on a mismatch, so the text pointer never moves backward.
The failure table encodes the longest proper prefix of the pattern that is also a suffix - it's what avoids re-scanning the text.

mcqs.q: KMP pattern matching runs in:
mcqs.explain: Linear in text plus pattern length.

mcqs.q: KMP avoids re-scanning text by precomputing:
options: The prefix (failure) function of the pattern
A suffix array of the text
mcqs.explain: It tells where to resume after a mismatch.

mcqs.q: In KMP, on a mismatch the TEXT pointer:
mcqs.explain: Only the pattern index falls back via the table.

u:dsa-strings-3-tries-prefix-trees.title: Tries (prefix trees)
u:dsa-strings-3-tries-prefix-trees.summary: A tree keyed by characters gives fast prefix search and autocomplete.

blocks.text: A **trie** stores strings as paths of characters from the root; shared prefixes share nodes. Insert and lookup of a word of length L are **O(L)**, independent of how many words are stored - ideal for autocomplete, spell-check, and prefix queries.
Mark end-of-word on nodes so you can distinguish a stored word from a mere prefix of a longer one.

mcqs.q: Looking up a word of length L in a trie is:
mcqs.explain: You walk one node per character.

mcqs.q: A trie is especially good at:
mcqs.explain: Shared prefixes make prefix search natural.

mcqs.q: To tell a full word from a prefix, a trie node stores:
options: The word count of the whole trie
mcqs.explain: The flag marks where a real word terminates.
